pedSummary.html:
Summary

Codeine is an opioid analgesic and antitussive used to treat mild to moderate pain and to reduce coughing. Codeine is no longer widely prescribed to pediatric patients due to cases of respiratory depression and death when used postoperatively following adenoidectomy and/or tonsillectomy. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a boxed warning that states that codeine is contraindicated in all children undergoing adenoidectomy and/or tonsillectomy and for any indication in children younger than 12 years old.

Pharmacogenomics Prescribing Information

The FDA drug label for codeine states that:

...individuals who are ultra-rapid metabolizers should not use Codeine Sulfate Tablets.

In addition, the Clinical Pharmacogenetic Implementation Consortium (CPIC) recommends that an alternative to codeine should be selected for CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers or poor metabolizers. These recommendations are applicable to both adult and pediatric patients.

CPIC has issued a 'no recommendation' for codeine dosing by OPRM1 and/or COMT genotype. From the guideline:

There is also insufficient evidence at this time to conclude altered analgesic response to other opioids in relation to rs1799971, or other OPRM1 variants.

For the most highly studied COMT variant, rs4680, there is no evidence to support an association of this variant with opioid adverse events, and there is mixed evidence for an association between COMT rs4680 genotype and analgesia or opioid dose requirements.

For all other COMT variants, there is mixed evidence for an association between COMT genotype and analgesia, opioid dose requirements or adverse events.

The Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group (DPWG) also recommends an alternative to codeine for CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers and gives recommendations for codeine in CYP2D6 poor metabolizers and intermediate metabolizers. Although the DPWG do not give any information specific to pediatric patients in their recommendations, they do not advise against applying these recommendations to pediatric patients.

Detailed annotations of all guidance for codeine can be found under the 'Prescribing Info' and 'Drug Label Annotations' tabs on this page.

Summary of Pharmacokinetics

To have a clinical effect, codeine must be metabolized into morphine, as depicted in codeine and morphine pathway by the enzyme CYP2D6. The ability of CYP2D6 to metabolize drugs varies between individuals due to variation in the CYP2D6 gene. Normal metabolizers (NMs) carry a combination of CYP2D6 alleles that result in normal CYP2D6 activity; these individuals will generally produce the expected amount of morphine from codeine. Intermediate metabolizers (IMs) have a combination of CYP2D6 alleles that result in lower CYP2D6 activity and will produce less morphine than expected. Poor metabolizers (PMs), individuals with two copies of the CYP2D6 gene that result in no CYP2D6 activity, may not benefit from codeine because it will not be metabolized into morphine. Ultrarapid metabolizers (UMs), those with CYP2D6 alleles that result in higher-than-normal CYP2D6 activity, may experience adverse effects due to increased morphine exposure.

Use In Specific Populations

Lactation

From the FDA drug label:

Women who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of codeine achieve higher than expected serum levels of morphine, potentially leading to higher levels of morphine in breast milk that can be dangerous in their breastfed infants. In women with normal codeine metabolism (normal CYP2D6 activity), the amount of codeine secreted into human milk is low and dose-dependent.

At least one death was reported in a nursing infant who was exposed to high levels of morphine in breast milk because the mother was an ultra-rapid metabolizer of codeine.

Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with Codeine Sulfate Tablets.

More information on codeine and breastfeeding can be found at the LactMed Database.

Pediatrics

Codeine is contraindicated by the FDA for postoperative analgesia in all children undergoing adenoidectomy and/or tonsillectomy. It is also contraindicated for pain control and cough reduction in children younger than 14 years and should be used with caution in children ages 14-18 years.

For more information on codeine in pediatric, pre-natal, and post-natal populations, please check the sidebar for the pediatric icon. Tabs with this icon contain information relevant to these populations.
